entries.reason: Mongoose's types cannot express a positional filter on an array element, which is what makes this backup-code consumption a compare-and-set rather than a read-then-write. The cast is documented in the four lines above it.

The form's schema is chosen at runtime from the item type, so `zodResolver(schema)` and the `control` it produces have no single static type. Narrowing them means one resolver per item type, which is the duplication the shared form exists to avoid.

entries.reason: The masking middleware is driven with hand-built request and response doubles carrying only the fields it reads; typing them as full Express objects would assert a shape the test deliberately does not provide. Two casts on one line, counted separately.

Focus-trap arithmetic over the focusable-element list. Each assertion is guarded by an explicit `length > 0` check on the line above; TypeScript cannot carry that narrowing across the index expression.
The fourth occurrence of the focus-trap assertion described in SUP-0004; policy.maxHitsPerEntry caps one entry at three, and splitting is the intended behaviour rather than raising the cap.

`while (true)` is the rejection-sampling loop that removes modular bias from the generator. The condition is provably constant and that is the point; the loop exits by `return` once an unbiased value is drawn.

Deliberate: the form compiles the user's own URI match pattern to check that it compiles at all, exactly as the stored schema does on read-back. Rejecting a pattern the schema would accept is the defect this avoids.
Pairs with SUP-0002: the runtime-selected resolver and control have no single static type, so the assignment cannot be proven safe without one resolver per item type.

The jsdom Web Crypto polyfill must be installed synchronously before any module under test reads `globalThis.crypto`, which an ESM import cannot guarantee inside a setup file.

TWO waits in an end-to-end spec, each buying a strictly later clock second after a password change so the token minted next is accepted: the `iat` vs `passwordChangedAt` comparison in middleware/auth.ts ceils a millisecond timestamp to the next second while a JWT `iat` has one-second precision, so a token minted in the same second is legitimately rejected. Both are load-bearing, measured: removing the first turned 'revoke refresh tokens after password change' red in 2 of 3 repeats, and removing the second turned 'preserve vault items after password change' red in 1 of 4. A THIRD occurrence was removed in Phase 19 rather than ledgered: 'change password and authenticate with new password' ends at the login response and never presents the token it mints, so the comparison never runs there - 3 of 3 repeats green without it. REMOVAL CONDITION CORRECTED IN PHASE 19. This entry used to name the injectable clock as its removal condition, alongside SUP-0021 to SUP-0024. That was wrong, and those four are now gone precisely because the clock DID reach them: they are vitest tests whose server runs in the same worker, so freezing Date there is seen by the code under test. These two are not. They are Playwright specs driving APIRequestContext, and the clock that must advance belongs to the API server in a SEPARATE PROCESS; no vitest fake reaches it, and page.clock fakes only the browser. The alternatives are worse than the debt: flooring passwordChangedAt to the second would open a one-second window in which a token issued before a password change is still accepted, which is a security regression, and a test phase may not change production behaviour. These are real waits on a real production property rather than concealed flakiness. Removed by an injectable clock the SERVER can be started with, or by an end-to-end harness able to advance the server's clock; neither exists today.

The E2E suite shares one dev server and one in-memory MongoDB across specs, so a second worker would race on both. It is a real constraint rather than a hidden flake, but it IS single-worker execution and the doctrine says to write that down. Phase 19 measures the flake rate and owns removing it; the short expiry is deliberate.

Phase 12 fixed an axe nested-interactive defect in VaultList: the row card carried role="button" with the selection checkbox INSIDE it, which makes the checkbox presentational and unreachable for assistive technology. Moving the activator to be a child of the card left the label a sibling of it, so the label's onClick={(e) => e.stopPropagation()} now stops propagation to nothing and was deleted. That arrow function is the one instrumentable line. The coverage scope is unchanged (packages/client/vitest.config.ts untouched), the measured file set is unchanged at 120 files, and no coverage percentage moved: line 98.69, branch 92.45, function 97.95 before and after. Keeping the handler purely to hold the denominator at 7038 would be dead code retained to satisfy a metric, which is the move this ledger exists to make visible.

test:resource's time and memory budgets can see a STEP CHANGE and nothing smaller, and this records how much smaller. Measured over five consecutive runs of the whole suite on an idle reference machine, the good runs themselves vary by 11-50 percent: rotation-volume rssGrowthMb spans 66.68-126.05 MB (50 percent of its median), backup-streaming durationMs spans 268-443 ms (49.7 percent), backup-full-vault durationMs 439-724 ms (47.1 percent). Every ceiling is therefore set at 1.6x-11x the observed maximum, which means a real regression smaller than roughly 1.7x on memory or 3x on time passes unseen. Shipping tighter numbers would produce a gate that fires on a loaded laptop, and a gate that fires for reasons unrelated to the code is a gate that gets deleted. ONE budget is exempt from this gap and is the reason the streaming scenario has a real verdict: backup-streaming rssGrowthMb, whose good band (43.43-58.11 MB over eleven runs) and regression band (118.54-156.41 MB over three runs of the find().lean() rewrite) do not overlap, so the 95 MB ceiling sits clear of both; and backup-streaming documentsDelivered, which measured 3320 of 10000 in eleven out of eleven runs against 10003 for the regression, with no spread at all. The gap is closed either by a metric with no noise band (a counter read from the server, as documentsDelivered is) or by a dedicated benchmark harness that controls for machine load; adding either is worth more than tightening these numbers.

entries.symbol: emailSchema's .trim() and its 'must have a TLD' refine
entries.reason: Twenty mutants in lines 1-27 of auth.ts are BEHAVIOURALLY EQUIVALENT rather than unasserted, and the reason is that the code they mutate is unreachable as a decider. emailSchema is z.email().max(254).toLowerCase().trim().refine(hasTld). The refine's own comment says zod accepts user@host, and that was true of the zod version it was written against; the installed zod 4 rejects it in z.email() itself, along with every other input the refine rejects. Its regex is anchored, admits no whitespace, forbids consecutive dots, requires each host label to start alphanumeric and requires a 2-or-more-letter TLD, so host.length === 0, host.startsWith('.'), host.endsWith('.'), labels.length < 2, an empty label and a label containing whitespace or an at sign are all already impossible by the time the refine runs. The same argument covers .trim(): a value with leading or trailing whitespace never reaches it. Verified structurally AND empirically - 1,248 addresses built from 6 local parts x 13 hosts x 4 leading x 4 trailing padding characters, comparing z.email().max(254).toLowerCase() against the full schema, produced ZERO disagreements in acceptance or in output. The code is KEPT rather than deleted, as defense-in-depth against a future loosening of zod's email format, on the same footing as toolsController's assertImportFieldLengths (which CLAUDE.md records as deliberately uncovered for the same reason). Removal condition: this entry goes away if zod's email check is ever replaced or loosened, at which point the refine becomes reachable and every one of these mutants becomes a missing assertion. What IS asserted, in tests/schema-bounds.test.ts, is the one transform that does change a value that reaches it: .toLowerCase(), which matters because the email is the PBKDF2 salt.

entries.symbol: formatBytes guards, normalizeUri optional-s, and the noUncheckedIndexedAccess fallbacks
entries.reason: Seven survivors in utils/index.ts are behaviourally equivalent, verified by REIMPLEMENTING each mutant beside the original and comparing outputs rather than by reading the code. (1) formatBytes line 12, 'bytes < 0' becoming 'bytes <= 0': zero is returned as '0 B' by the very next line either way. (2) formatBytes line 13, the 'bytes === 0' early return deleted: Math.log(0) is -Infinity, which the Math.max(...,0) clamp on line 21 turns into exponent 0, so the function still returns '0 B'. Both compared over 334 values - every power of two from 2^-40 to 2^63 and its neighbours, plus 0, -0, negatives, Infinity, NaN, Number.MIN_VALUE, Number.EPSILON and each unit boundary - with ZERO disagreements. The early return is kept because it states the intent at the top rather than leaving it to a clamp four lines down. (3) normalizeUri line 32, '/^(https?:|mailto:)/i' becoming '/^(https:|mailto:)/i': an http: URI that stops matching the first guard is caught by the SECOND guard on line 34 ('some other scheme, leave it alone') and returned unchanged, so the two are indistinguishable from outside; compared over 15 scheme shapes with zero disagreements. What is NOT equivalent, and is now asserted in tests/utils.test.ts, is either ANCHOR being dropped from either pattern. (4) Three NoCoverage mutants on the '?? ' and "?? 'B'" fallbacks at lines 6, 7 and 22: these exist to satisfy noUncheckedIndexedAccess and are unreachable - local[0] and local[local.length-1] are defined whenever atIndex > 0, and sizes[i] is defined because i is clamped to the array's own length. CLAUDE.md already records this class as deliberately uncovered ('noUncheckedIndexedAccess nullish guards'), and lighting them up would need a contrived mock of an index operation. Removal condition: (1)-(3) go away if the guards they duplicate are removed; (4) goes away if the compiler stops requiring the fallback.

Testing-matrix row S12 (software bill of materials) is APPLICABLE — this project ships a deployed artifact — and is deferred on marginal value rather than on relevance. The dependency surface is already gated three ways: `audit:deps` fails on any advisory at moderate or above across the production tree, `audit:licenses` holds every production dependency to `.licenses-allowlist.json`, and `audit:image` runs Trivy over all three images. An SBOM would add provenance and downstream consumability, neither of which has a consumer for a self-hosted single-image application today. Removal condition: this entry goes away when a published SBOM has a consumer — a distribution channel, a compliance requirement, or a downstream packager — at which point `syft`/`cyclonedx` output belongs in the release workflow beside the GitHub Release.

Testing-matrix row B9 (visual regression) is APPLICABLE in principle to any UI, so a 'not applicable' would not be earned by a fact. It is deferred because there is no protected design contract to regress against, and because function — the thing a screenshot diff is a proxy for — is already covered directly: `test:a11y` runs axe over fifteen views and asserts the keyboard invariants, the component suites assert rendered output, and the E2E suite drives the real journeys. A pixel baseline added now would mostly report intended CSS churn. Removal condition: a stable design system, or a recurrence of a defect that only a rendered diff would have caught.

Testing-matrix row N1 (performance) is deferred on SCOPE, and the honest statement is that its noise band is UNKNOWN rather than too wide — no benchmark was run during the audit, and the doctrine licenses a noise-based deferral only after five or more runs with the spread recorded. What exists instead is `test:resource`, which holds four volume scenarios over a 10,000-item vault to committed time and memory ceilings; SUP-0027 records exactly how coarse those ceilings are and why. Removal condition: a dedicated benchmark harness that controls for machine load, which SUP-0027 also names as the better of the two ways to close its own gap.

Testing-matrix row N2 (load) is deferred because H-Vault is a self-hosted, single-tenant deployment and no concurrent-user SLO exists to test against. A load test with no target measures the machine it runs on. Removal condition: a multi-tenant or hosted deployment mode, which would create the SLO this row needs in order to mean anything.

Testing-matrix row N3 (stress) is deferred for the same reason as N2: single-tenant self-hosted deployment, no concurrent-user SLO, therefore no defined breaking point to drive toward. The per-user ceilings that DO bound this application — MAX_ITEMS_PER_USER, MAX_FOLDERS_PER_USER, the body-size limits — are exercised at their maximum by `test:resource` and by the schema bounds suites. Removal condition: as N2.

Testing-matrix row N4 (spike) is deferred for the same reason as N2 and N3. The one burst-shaped behaviour that does have a defined contract — the rate limiters — is asserted directly against a real MongoDB-backed store rather than by traffic generation, including the fail-closed path and the IPv6 /64 aggregation. Removal condition: as N2.

Testing-matrix row N5 (soak) is deferred on scope rather than on an established noise band, exactly as N1 is: no long-running measurement was taken, so no leak rate is known. `test:resource` records RSS growth per scenario, which is a single-operation reading and not a substitute for a multi-hour soak. Removal condition: the same benchmark harness N1 needs, run over a long window.

Testing-matrix row N10 (degraded network) is deferred because the behaviour it targets is already covered where it matters: the offline path has direct tests over the IndexedDB cache and the PWA service worker, and the Axios layer's retry, refresh-serialisation and session-failure branches are unit-tested against injected failures rather than against injected latency. Deliberate latency injection adds little for an application whose primary deployment is a LAN or a single host. Removal condition: a hosted deployment mode, or a defect traced to timing that only throttling would reproduce.

Testing-matrix row R2 (chaos) is deferred because the topology has no surface for it: one datastore, no service mesh, no inter-service RPC to sever. The failure modes that DO exist here are tested directly and violently by `test:recovery`, which SIGKILLs a real process at five injection points around the key rotation and the import, and reaps the transactions the dead process left open. Removal condition: a second stateful service, or any deployment topology with a network partition worth injecting.

Testing-matrix row R6 (reliability: MTBF/MTTR measurement) folds into N5 and is deferred with it — both need a long-running observation window that has never been run. The recoverability half of reliability, which is the half that matters for a password manager, is covered by `test:recovery`'s backup-restore drill onto a second database and by `test:deploy`'s restart-and-re-sign-in check. Removal condition: as N5.

Testing-matrix row D6 (compatibility) is deferred because the runtime is pinned rather than ranged: Node 24 in `.nvmrc`, in `engines.node` (>=24.0.0) and in every image, so there is no supported matrix to test across. The README records the dropped Node 22 leg as a known gap on the same grounds. The Windows leg cannot run on this machine at all. Removal condition: widening `engines.node`, or publishing support for a second platform — either creates the matrix this row is about.

Testing-matrix row X2 (dynamic application security testing) is deferred on value ordering, not on relevance: a ZAP baseline against the local stack is feasible — `test:deploy` already stands the whole Compose stack up and drives a journey through its single published port, so the target exists. It sits below the matrix because the classes a baseline scan finds are covered statically and by direct assertion here: the security headers and CSP are asserted per response, the cross-user authorization matrix covers every id-taking route, CSRF is constant-time double-submit with its own suite, and `audit:sast` runs the CodeQL security-and-quality suite over the source. Removal condition: this is the strongest remaining candidate of the deferred rows — wire ZAP baseline into the deploy drill once the stack is already up.

Testing-matrix row B10 is the one row the audit UPGRADED from DEFERRED to 'APPLICABLE: missing' on review, so this entry records a commitment with a short clock, not a dismissal. `playwright.config.ts` declares a single `chromium` project, so every browser assertion this project makes is an assertion about one engine. That matters most for exactly one subsystem: `services/clipboard/clipboardService.ts` is built around the fact that Chromium refuses `writeText` from an unfocused document while Firefox and Safari require transient activation for EVERY write — its refusal-retry state machine and the gesture listeners in `useClipboardGuard` exist for the non-Chromium case and are verified only by unit tests with simulated refusals. It is not being taken during release preparation because a first cross-browser leg is as likely to report a genuine Firefox difference as a passing run, and the honest response to that is a fix rather than a release delay or a weakened gate. Removal condition: a `firefox` project running at minimum the clipboard-hygiene and auto-lock specs, added as its own reported leg so a cross-browser failure is attributable.

`test:a11y` scans the LIGHT theme only, so the dark palette is unmeasured, and one defect in it is already known and reproduced: dark `--destructive` (0 62.8% 30.6%) is a dark red that cannot reach 4.5:1 as TEXT on the near-black `--background` (222.2 84% 4.9%). It is used 83 times across 25 client files, 65 of those as text and 8 as a solid button background under the near-white `--destructive-foreground` — two roles that pull the lightness in opposite directions, so no single token can satisfy both and the repair is a second, text-only token plus 65 call-site edits. The light theme was fixed with measured ratios and is verified by `e2e/a11y.spec.ts`; the comment above the token in globals.css records the dark case rather than half-fixing it. This is deliberately NOT being taken during release preparation: extending the scan to the dark theme first is the correct order, and it is expected to surface further palette failures beyond this one (the audit notes `text-*-600` in roughly thirty more places), each needing a design decision rather than a token tweak. Removal condition: a dark-theme leg added to the a11y gate, and the token split that makes it pass.

entries.symbol: the absent `mutation` block, and the verify:full run that fails without it
entries.reason: `test:mutation` is registered at tier 2 and has no recorded floor, so it exits 1 with 'no mutation block in baseline.json — this run held no floor' and `npm run verify:full` cannot pass. `npm run ci:local`, the clean room, is blocked by the same thing and for a sharper reason: it runs `verify:full` inside a fresh worktree, which has no Stryker incremental files, so it would start a from-scratch multi-hour mutation run and then fail on the missing floor regardless. It is therefore not being run either, and the last clean-room evidence predates this release. That is the gate's deliberate bootstrap behaviour, not a defect: a gate that passes having compared its result against nothing is not a gate. `npm run ci` — the tier-0 and tier-1 surface the pre-push hook and the release workflow both run — is unaffected and green, which is why a release can still be cut. Progress so far, all of it preserved in `.stryker-tmp/` so a later run resumes incrementally rather than repeating: the shared leg is complete (79.9% over 2,008 mutants, survivors triaged as SUP-0028 and SUP-0029) and the client leg is complete (74.57% over 15,322 mutants, 3,642 survivors, 12h35m). The server leg is NOT: its dry run died on `batch7-fixes.test.ts`'s HIBP cache test at the 30-second timeout, a test that measures 7.3 s on a free machine, because an unrelated project's test suite was saturating all four cores at the time. That same contention is why neither completed leg is being banked: a test starved of CPU fails on a timeout, Stryker records a timeout as a KILLED mutant, and a floor inflated that way is one a clean run can never clear — the client leg's 52 timeouts are the suspect population. Removal condition, in order: re-run the server leg on a verifiably idle machine, re-test the client leg's timeout mutants and re-run that leg with `--full` if any survive when given a core, then `npm run test:mutation` and `node scripts/ci/ratchet-check.mjs --accept`. Triage of the ~3,900 survivors raises the floor afterwards and is not a precondition for recording it.
